events.title: The September 11 attacks
events.description: Terrorist attacks kill thousands of people in the United States. Communities mourn and help those affected.

events.title: Apple introduces the iPod
events.description: A pocket-sized digital music player becomes a new product for the computer maker.

events.title: Microsoft and the US government propose a settlement
events.description: The agreement would restrict some business practices. Court review and other legal steps remain.

events.title: Euro cash enters everyday use
events.description: Twelve countries introduce euro notes and coins.

events.title: Columbia is lost
events.description: The space shuttle breaks apart during its return to Earth, killing its seven crew members.

what_happened_next.text:
Apple gained about two-fifths over five years, while Cisco lost about seven-tenths and Microsoft also fell. Bonds gained while the US basket ended lower. Being in the broad technology industry did not give these three companies the same result. Even Apple’s final gain hid a very rough journey.

In November 2001, Microsoft and the US government proposed a settlement of their competition case. The legal story had moved forward, though review was still required.

Apple introduced the iPod in October 2001, expanding beyond computers into portable music. The business itself was changing while investors held its shares.

The years ahead included the September 11 attacks, the introduction of euro cash and the Columbia shuttle disaster. People faced changes and losses far beyond their investment accounts. The monthly lines show the financial result, which is only one part of that larger history.

Apple’s final gain is especially worth comparing with its path. Finishing above the starting point does not mean an investment never fell below it. A person who had to sell during a bad month would not receive the five-year ending value. Likewise, a lawsuit or a promising device could not tell someone exactly when prices would turn. The uncertainty was present even for the investment that eventually gained.

reflection.what_people_were_focused_on: Korean diplomacy, digital music and Microsoft’s court case were prominent. People were also discovering new museums and returning to everyday hobbies.
reflection.what_actually_mattered: Different businesses and asset types mattered more than one broad label such as technology. A portfolio concentrated in a few famous names faced large company risks.
reflection.what_faded_away: The first reaction to a court order did not explain the complete investment result. Neither did the latest online trading tool.
reflection.what_nobody_knew: The precise winners and losses were unknown. An investor could not know in advance how a promising product, a lawsuit or a major world event would affect the final value.

hot_stock_outcomes.text: Microsoft grew after the technology-stock slump. By the year ending June 2005, annual sales reached $39.79 billion and profit reached $12.25 billion. Businesses bought more SQL Server software, and Xbox sales also grew. Microsoft paid cash to shareholders and bought back some of its shares. Even so, the investment finished below its June 2000 value.

Cisco’s customers cut technology spending sharply in 2001. Cisco had bought too many parts for orders that never came. It cut their recorded value by $2.2 billion. Sales later recovered to $22 billion in the year ending July 2004, with $4.4 billion in profit. The company recovered faster than its share price, which remained far below the 2000 level.

Apple’s early computer slump made this a rough ride. The 2000 holiday quarter produced a $195 million loss as Apple cleared excess stock. The iPod arrived in October 2001 and later became a hit: Apple shipped 4.58 million in the 2004 holiday quarter. Company profit reached $295 million that quarter, helping the shares climb back above their starting point.
